standard_prerequisites.name: Brenier duality for optimal transport into two separated convex targets
standard_prerequisites.statement: The transport potentials u and v are globally Lipschitz convex functions linked by the dual formulas v(y) = sup over x in Omega of (y dot x minus u(x)) and u-sub-i(x) = sup over y in Omega-sub-i-star of (y dot x minus v(y)), the singular set is the interface where u-one and u-two agree, and the target domains Omega-sub-i-star are convex and separated by a hyperplane.
standard_prerequisites.use: Fixes the objects of the counted statement: the point y-zero is the image of the singular point under the gradient of u-one, Omega-sub-one-star is the target component whose boundary is touched there, and the width is measured inside that component.

standard_prerequisites.name: Caffarelli regularity and the geometry of centred sections
standard_prerequisites.statement: Under the Monge-Ampere density bounds the centred sections of v are convex, have centre of mass at their centre point, are of geometric decay, and satisfy the strict convexity estimate recalled in the retained context; the volume of a centred section at height h is comparable to h to the power n over two.
standard_prerequisites.use: The retained volume estimate and the retained tangential estimate are the two inputs of the counted proof, and the retained equivalence between sub-level sets and centred sections converts the width statement into a volume statement.

standard_prerequisites.name: Elementary convex geometry: Hausdorff measure, convex hulls and uniform convexity
standard_prerequisites.statement: The two-dimensional Hausdorff measure of a planar region bounded by a uniformly convex arc and a chord is at least a constant times the three-halves power of the chord height, the convex hull of that region with points at a controlled tangential distance is contained in any convex set containing both, and on a uniformly convex boundary a displacement in the normal direction is at least a constant times the square of the tangential displacement.
standard_prerequisites.use: These three elementary facts are the substance of the two halves of the counted proof: the lower bound for the measure of the planar region, and the final uniform convexity inequality relating the tangential width to the normal width.

core_obligations: Set up the objects of the width estimate: with p the point of the closure of the intersection of the centred section S-superscript-c-sub-h of v at y-zero with Omega-sub-one-star maximising the displacement in the direction e-one, write q for the intersection of the segment from the origin to p with the boundary of Omega-sub-one-star, and use convexity to place q in the closure of the section intersected with that boundary (source lines 846-849).

Translate the width into a normal displacement: from convergence of the intersection to y-zero, obtain q-sub-n over p-sub-n at least one half for small h, hence q-one at least one half of the normal width d at e-one, and define the unit vector e-sub-q pointing from y-zero to q (source lines 850-854).

Bound the planar region below: let D be the planar region inside the span of e-sub-q and e-one bounded by the boundary of Omega-sub-one-star and the segment from y-zero to q; uniform convexity of that boundary gives a two-dimensional Hausdorff measure of D of at least a constant times the three-halves power of the normal width (source lines 855-858).

Build a three-dimensional convex hull of controlled volume: choose an orthonormal basis of the orthogonal complement of the span of e-one and e-sub-p, use the retained tangential estimate to place points at tangential distance a constant times h to the power one half plus epsilon from y-zero in the centred section at height b h, and take the convex hull G of D with those points; convexity puts G inside the centred section at height b h (source lines 860-863).

Compare volumes and read off the exponent: the volume of G is at least a constant times h to the power (one half plus epsilon) times (n minus two) times the measure of D, while the volume of the centred section is comparable to h to the power n over two; cancelling the powers of h gives the normal width bound with exponent two thirds minus epsilon (source lines 865-869).

Prove the second claim: for a unit vector e in the span of e-two up to e-sub-n, uniform convexity of the boundary of Omega-sub-one-star gives that the normal width is at least a constant times the square of the tangential displacement, which is the asserted bound of the squared tangential width by the normal width (source lines 871-873).

proof_roadmap.step: Choose the maximising point p, move to the boundary point q of the target component and convert the normal width into a normal displacement along the boundary.
Bound the area of the planar region D by uniform convexity and thicken it, using the tangential estimate, into a convex hull G contained in the centred section at height b h.
Compare the volume of G with the volume of the centred section and solve for the normal width, obtaining the exponent two thirds minus epsilon.
Use uniform convexity once more to bound the squared tangential width by the normal width.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the lemma labelled ide1 at source lines 838-844: for a centred section of the potential v at the singular point's image y-zero, the maximal displacement d at e-one inside the target component obeys d at most a constant times h to the power two thirds minus epsilon, and every tangential width has its square bounded by that normal width. The proof is a volume comparison whose two sides must be matched in the right scale: the planar region D cut off by the uniformly convex boundary of Omega-sub-one-star contributes a factor of the three-halves power of the normal width (source lines 855-858), while thickening it by the tangential points at distance a constant times h to the power one half plus epsilon, taken from the tangential regularity of v at the base point, contributes the factor h to the power (one half plus epsilon) times (n minus two) (source lines 860-863). Comparing that product with the volume of the centred section, which is comparable to h to the power n over two (source lines 865-869), is exactly what produces the exponent two thirds minus epsilon, and it is the balance of the exponent one half plus epsilon from the tangential estimate against the inverse-square-law exponent from uniform convexity that makes the claim true. The second half of the statement is a different estimate, obtained by the uniform convexity inequality that turns a tangential displacement into a normal one (source lines 871-873). Nothing in the article before this point supplies the width bound, and neither a single-scaled barrier argument nor the volume estimate alone reaches it.
